L000103	\begin{abstract}
L000104	First passage phenomena arise across physics, biology, and finance when stochastic processes first reach a threshold, triggering downstream events. Examples include the irreversible exit from a domain, a biochemical reaction, a financial selloff. While typical formulations involve diffusive motion, many stochastic processes are better described as velocity jump processes, characterized by persistent motion interrupted by stochastic velocity changes. Despite their ubiquity, first-passage properties of velocity jump processes remain underdeveloped in higher dimensions, especially under directional bias. We present a general framework to estimate the mean first passage time (MFPT) and higher moments of the survival probability for fixed-speed velocity jump processes where possible reorientations range from strong alignment to full angular anisotropy. For low Knudsen numbers, when the mean free path is small compared to the distance to the target, we derive a universal form for the MFPT in which two bias functions encode broad classes of angular distributions, including von Mises–Fisher, wrapped Cauchy, and elliptical families. In the narrow capture limit of a vanishingly small target, directional persistence induces anomalous scaling, including regimes where the MFPT remains finite whereas standard diffusion would predict divergence. Finally, we obtain a Langevin representation that accurately reproduces first-passage statistics. Analytical predictions are confirmed
L000105	by numerical simulations.
L000106	\end{abstract}
L000107	
L000108	
L000109	
L000110	\maketitle
L000111	
L000112	
L000113	Velocity jump processes capture a wide range of realistic non-diffusive
L000114	behaviors \cite{VanKampen1981, Klages2008}.
L000115	Examples include molecular collisions in biochemistry \cite{Hanggi1990},
L000116	run-and-tumble motion in bacteria \cite{Newby2011,Scacchi2018, Dhar2019, Angelani2014,iyaniwura2025meanpassagetimeactive},
L000117	pricing in quantitative finance \cite{Bielecki2004, Masoliver2008, Perello2011},
L000118	animal movement \cite{Fauchald2003, Benichou2011, Kurella2015, Costa2024}.
L000119	In all cases, the items of interest ``run" along a given direction for a random time
L000120	until a new velocity is selected.
L000121	The resulting dynamics is intermittent directed motion that can significantly differ from standard
L000122	diffusion due to the inherent persistence.
L000123	Velocity jumps may arise from internal mechanisms,
L000124	external perturbations, or in response to sensory cues.
L000125	The best known
L000126	representation of this paradigm
L000127	are the one-dimensional telegrapher equations
L000128	that are commonly used to study run-and-tumble behaviors \cite{Heaviside1970, hillen2013transport,HillenReview,Angelani2015}.
L000129	
L000130	Non-equilibrium first-passage properties of jump processes
L000131	are of great significance and may be even more important than
L000132	steady-state quantities such as
L000133	moments of the mean displacement or particle distributions \cite{Datta2024}.
L000134	For example, the mean first passage time (MFPT), defined as
L000135	the average time to first reach a target  \cite{Redner2001}, informs
L000136	how long one must wait for downstream, often irreversible, events to
L000137	be initiated, such as immune responses, biochemical transformations,
L000138	entry into subcellular compartments \cite{Ghusinga2017, Dorsogna2009, Nowak2009},
L000139	escape from an enclosed domain \cite{Condamin2008, Bressloff2013, Gardiner2004}.
L000140	The time to reach a threshold is also used as a measure
L000141	of resilience in ecology \cite{Arani2021} or to quantify the onset of
L000142	mental health disorders \cite{Mao2024}.
L000143	Understanding how persistence and directionality
L000144	affect
L000145	first passage phenomena is critical  \cite{
L000146	Camley2014, Sevilla2019, Artuso2018, Klinger2023, Vezzani2024};
L000147	however, the problem is notoriously difficult in
L000148	higher dimensions because velocities can reorient
L000149	along a continuum of directions, and
L000150	not just to the left or right
L000151	as in $d=1$  \cite{Rupprecht2016, Grebenkov2016, Mori2020}.
L000152	
L000153	
L000154	The aim of this Letter is to help fill this gap.
L000155	We write a general equation for the MFPT $\Theta({\bf x},{\bf {v}})$
L000156	to a given target for a particle starting at position ${\bf {x}}$ with velocity ${\bf {v}}$ under a velocity jump process
L000157	where jumps occur at rate $\mu$ and where $q({\bf {x}},{\bf {v}})$ is the memoryless probability
L000158	density function for a particle at  ${\bf {x}}$ to switch to velocity ${\bf {v}}$.
L000159	In many settings the speed $v$ is fixed,
L000160	to a physiological value in biology or to the thermal velocity in Brownian motion for example,
L000161	so that the jump process becomes a series
L000162	of stochastic reorientations.  The turning angle may be completely random,
L000163	as in run-and-tumble systems,
L000164	or may bias the motion along a preferred direction, as when there is an underlying
L000165	network, external field or chemical trail. For fixed speed
L000166	$ v  = \sigma$ and
L000167	small Knudsen number $\varepsilon = \sigma / (\mu L)  \ll 1$,
L000168	where $\sigma / \mu$ is the mean free path and $L$ is a characteristic distance
L000169	the particle must travel before reaching the target or escaping the domain,
L000170	we show that $\Theta({{\bf {x}}},{\bf {v}}) \sim T({\bf {x}}) + {\cal O}(\varepsilon)$
L000171	and write a self-contained differential equation for $T({\bf {x}})$
L000172	valid in $d$-dimensional systems.
L000173	We solve for $T({\bf {x}})$ under
L000174	representative turning angle distributions in simple geometries
L000175	and compare our results with numerical simulations for $d=2, 3$.
L000176	
L000177	
L000178	The probability density $P ({\bf {x}}, {\bf {v}}, t)$
L000179	to be at position ${\bf {x}}$ with velocity ${\bf {v}}$ at time $t$ obeys the forward equation
L000180	
L000181	\begin{equation}
L000182	\label{forward}
L000183	\frac{\partial P }{\partial t}  + {\bf {v}} \cdot  \nabla P = - \mu P +  \mu \int q({\bf {x}},{\bf {v}}) P({\bf {x}}, {\bf{v}'}, t) d \bf{v}'
L000184	\end{equation}
L000185	
L000186	for given initial and boundary conditions.
L000187	The integral is over the chosen velocity domain
L000188	of $q({\bf {x}}, {\bf {v}})$.
L000189	The survival probability
L000190	$S({\bf {x}}, {\bf {v}},t)$ for a particle initiated
L000191	at $({\bf {x}}, {\bf{v}})$ to remain in a spatial domain
L000192	$\cal D$ without having reached a specified target at time $t$ follows the backward
L000193	Kolmogorov equation, given
L000194	by the adjoint of Eq.\,\ref{forward}
L000195	
L000196	\begin{equation}
L000197	\label{backward}
L000198	\frac{\partial S }{\partial t}  - {\bf {v}} \cdot  \nabla S = - \mu S +  \mu \int q({\bf {x}},{\bf{v}}') S({\bf {x}}, {\bf{v}'}, t) d \bf{v}',
L000199	\end{equation}
L000200	
L000201	where $S({\bf {x}}, {\bf {v}}, 0) =1$ for all ${\bf {x}}$ in $\cal{D}$ and any $\bf v$.
L000202	Eq.\,\ref{backward} is solved with
L000203	absorbing boundaries at the
L000204	target and reflecting elsewhere; more details are
L000205	given in the Supplemental Material (SM).
L000206	The escape probability $1 - S$ yields the first-passage time probability density
L000207	 $-{\partial S}/ {\partial t}$. The MFPT $\Theta({\bf {x}}, {\bf {v}})$ is its first moment
L000208	
L000209	\begin{equation}
L000210	\label{moment}
L000211	\Theta({\bf {x}}, {\bf {v}}) = - \int_{0}^{\infty} t \frac{\partial S} {\partial t} dt =  \int_{0}^{\infty} S( {\bf {x}}, {\bf {v}}, t) dt.
L000212	\end{equation}
L000213	
L000214	Integrating Eq.\,\ref{backward} over time yields
L000215	
L000216	\begin{equation}
L000217	\label{MFPTgen}
L000218	-1  - {\bf {v}} \cdot  \nabla \Theta = - \mu \Theta +  \mu \int q({\bf {x}},{\bf {v}}') \Theta({\bf {x}}, {\bf {v}}') d {\bf {v}}'.
L000219	\end{equation}
L000220	
L000221	Upon multiplying Eq.\,\ref{MFPTgen} by $q({\bf {x}}, {\bf {v}})$ and
L000222	by $\bf {v} \, q({\bf {x}}, {\bf {v}})$,  integrating both expressions
L000223	over velocity space, and merging results one obtains
L000224	
L000225	\begin{eqnarray}
L000226	\nonumber
L000227	-1 &=& \frac{1}{\mu} \int q({\bf {x}}, {\bf {v}}) ({\bf {v}}  \, \otimes \, {\bf {v}} :
L000228	\nabla \, \otimes \, \nabla) \Theta({\bf {x}}, {\bf {v}})  \, d {\bf {v}} + \\
L000229	\label{MFPT}
L000230	&&  {\bf {b}}( {\bf {x}})\cdot {\nabla} \int q({\bf {x}}, {\bf {v}}) \,\Theta ({\bf {x}}, {\bf {v}}) d {\bf {v}}.
L000231	\end{eqnarray}
L000232	
L000233	Here $\otimes$ represents the tensor product
L000234	between vectors and the colon their convolution, so that
L000235	in dimension $d$
L000236	
L000237	\begin{eqnarray}
L000238	\nonumber
L000239	{\bf {v}}  \, \otimes \, {\bf {v}} :
L000240	\nabla \, \otimes \, \nabla =  \sum_{i,j = \{1,2, \dots, d \}} v_i v_j \frac{\partial}{\partial{x_i}} \frac{\partial}{\partial{x_j}},
L000241	\end{eqnarray}
L000242	
L000243	and ${\bf {b}} ({\bf {x}})$ is a drift term given by
L000244	
L000245	\begin{eqnarray}
L000246	\label{drift}
L000247	{\bf {b}} ({\bf {x}}) = \int {\bf {v}} \, q({\bf {x}}, {\bf {v}}) d {\bf {v}}.
L000248	\end{eqnarray}
L000249	
L000250	If $q({\bf {x}}, {\bf {v}}) = q({\bf {x}}, -{\bf {v}})$
L000251	reorientation is symmetric in ${\bf v}$ and ${\bf {b}} ({\bf {x}}) =0$ \cite{Hillen2025}.
L000252	We now fix the speed $v = \sigma$. For $d=1$
L000253	Eqs.\,\ref{forward} and \ref{backward} yield the
L000254	 telegrapher's equations with $q(x, \sigma) = q(x,-\sigma) = 1/2$
L000255	\cite{Weiss2002, Weiss1994, Hemmer1961, Kac1974, DOrsogna2003}.
L000256	For $d >1 $,
L000257	we set ${\bf v} = \sigma \, \hat \theta$, where
L000258	$\hat \theta $ is the unit vector along the direction of motion. We write
L000259	$q({\bf {x}}, {\bf {v}}) = q({\bf {x}}, \hat \theta) \, \delta(v - \sigma) / \sigma^{d-1} $
L000260	where $q({\bf {x}}, \hat \theta)$ is the reorientation distribution and
L000261	denote the angular volume element $d \hat \theta_{d-1}$ so that
L000262	$\int q({\bf {x}}, \hat \theta) d \hat \theta_{d-1} = \int q({\bf {x}}, {\bf {v}}) d {\bf {v}} = 1$ and
L000263	${\bf {b}}({\bf {x}}) = \sigma \int \hat \theta q({{\bf {x}}}, \hat \theta) d \hat \theta_{d-1}$.
L000264	Using the non-dimensional variables ${\bm \xi} = {\bf {x}}/L$,
L000265	$\tau = \sigma^2 t / (\mu L^2)$, with $L$ a typical length scale, we rewrite
L000266	Eq.\,\ref{backward} as
L000267	
L000268	\begin{figure}[t!]
L000269	\includegraphics[width=0.35\textwidth]{VonMises_6fig.png}
L000270	\caption{
L000271	The von Mises angular distribution in Eq.\,\ref{VM} for $d=2$ and three
L000272	values of the concentration $\kappa(\bf x)$ that quantifies the
L000273	bias towards $\hat \gamma(\bx)$.
L000274	Larger $\kappa (\bf x)$ yields sharper alignment.}
L000275	\end{figure}
L000276	
L000277	\begin{equation}
L000278	\label{backwardres}
L000279	\varepsilon^2 \frac{\partial S }{\partial \tau}  - \varepsilon \, \hat \theta \cdot  \nabla_{{\bm {\xi}}} S = - S +   \int q({\bm {\xi}}, \hat \theta) S({\bm {\xi}}, \hat \theta, \tau) d \hat \theta_{d-1}.
L000280	\end{equation}
L000281	
L000282	Here, $\varepsilon = \ell/ L$ is the Knudsen number and $\ell = \sigma/\mu$ the mean free path. We now assume $\varepsilon \ll 1$.
L000283	Due to the drift term, a standard asymptotic expansion is insufficient,  so we separate fast and slow time scales
L000284	by introducing $z = \tau/ \varepsilon$ and pose
L000285	$S({\bm {\xi}}, \hat \theta,\tau) = S_0({\bm {\xi}}, \hat \theta, \tau) +
L000286	\varepsilon S_1({\bm {\xi}}, \hat \theta, \tau)  + \dots$  where
L000287	 $S_i({\bm {\xi}}, \hat \theta,\tau) = s_i({\bm {\xi}}, \hat \theta, \tau, z)$ \cite{Bender1999}.
L000288	The initial condition $S({\bf {x}}, {\bf {v}}, 0) =1$ for all ${\bf {x}}$ in $\cal D$
L000289	for any $\bf v$ maps to $s_i({\bm {\xi}}, \hat \theta, 0,0)= 0$ for $i \neq 0$ and
L000290	 $s_0({\bm {\xi}}, \hat \theta, 0,0)= 1$. Thus,
L000291	
L000292	\begin{eqnarray}
L000293	\label{derivativeres}
L000294	\frac{\partial S} {\partial \tau} = \frac 1 {\varepsilon} \frac{\partial s_0}  {\partial z} +
L000295	 \left( \frac{\partial s_0}{\partial \tau } + \frac{\partial s_1} {\partial z} \right)+
L000296	\dots
L000297	 \end{eqnarray}
L000298	
L000299	By inserting Eq.\,\ref{derivativeres} into Eq.\,\ref{backwardres},
L000300	matching orders in $\varepsilon$ and returning to $\tau$,
L000301	we find that $S_0({\bm {\xi}}, \tau)$  is independent
L000302	of $\hat \theta$ and that the integral $\int_0^{\infty} S_0 ({\bm {\xi}}, \tau) d\tau$ satisfies a self-consistent differential equation.
L000303	This integral is the rescaled MFPT to leading order.  Rewriting it in dimensional units, $T({\bf {x}}) = (\mu L^2 /\sigma^2) \int_0^{\infty} S_0 ({\bf {x}}, \tau) d\tau $, yields a self-consistent differential equation for $T({\bf x})$,
L000304	valid for $\varepsilon \ll 1$, given by
L000305	\begin{eqnarray}
L000306	\label{superfinal}
L000307	{\mathbb D}({\bf {x}}) : \nabla \otimes \nabla \,
L000308	T({\bf {x}})
L000309	+ {\bf {b}}({\bf {x}}) \cdot \nabla \, T({\bf {x}}) = -1,
L000310	\end{eqnarray}
L000311	
L000312	where the diffusion tensor ${\mathbb D}({\bf {x}})$ is defined as
L000313	
L000314	\begin{eqnarray}
L000315	\label{difftensor}
L000316	{\mathbb D}({\bf {x}}) = \frac{\sigma^2}{\mu} \int  q ({\bf {x}}, \hat \theta) \hat \theta \otimes \hat \theta \,  d \hat \theta_{d-1},
L000317	\end{eqnarray}
L000318	
L000319	and $T({\bf x}) =0$ at the target. Eq.\,\ref{superfinal} is one of our main findings and coincides with Eq.\,\ref{MFPT} for $v = \sigma$ and $\Theta({\bf {x}}, {\bf v})= T({\bf x})$.
L000320	It is more general than previous results as it allows directional asymmetries and a non-zero drift.
L000321	More details are in the SM. Locally, interpreting $L$ as the distance between the starting point and the target,
L000322	Eq.\,\ref{superfinal}
L000323	implies that the MFPT is independent of the initial orientation
L000324	if the distance to the target is much larger than the mean free path.
L000325	In this case, the many particle reorientations erase memory of the initial heading. The full kinetic description in
L000326	Eq.\,\ref{MFPT} must be retained if instead
L000327	the initial position is at ${\cal O}(\ell)$ from the target.

L000664	Our results have broad applications. As shown in the SM, the von Mises kernel in Eq.\,\ref{VM}
L000665	is the steady-state distribution of an overdamped angular system driven by the
L000666	potential $U(\theta, {\bf x}) = - \tau_{\rm M}({\bf x})  \cos (\theta - \gamma({\bf x}))$,
L000667	where the torque biases orientation along $\hat \gamma({\bf x})$ in competition with
L000668	rotational noise \cite{Hofling2025}, leading to $\kappa({\bf x}) \propto \tau_{\rm M}({\bf x})$. Assuming an electric field of magnitude $E({\bf x})$ directed along $\hat \gamma({\bf x})$, we can model $\tau_{\rm M}({\bf x}) \propto E({\bf x})$,
L000669	so that $\kappa({\bf x}) \propto E({\bf x})$.
L000670	Thus, Eq.\,\ref{VM} arises as a natural way to describe field-driven motion.
L000671	For $d=2$, radial guidance and a uniform, weak $E$
L000672	Eq.\,\ref{scaling1} yields $\tau_{\rm g} \sim \zeta^{\nu}$ with $\nu \propto E^2$, providing an avenue to
L000673	test the predicted scaling. For behavioral systems, without physical torques, Eq.\,\ref{VM} can still be used to
L000674	model transport biased by trails, social cues, or learning.
L000675	From this perspective, as discussed in the SM, our work offers a unified framework
L000676	in which to study the MFPT of field-driven colloidal matter,  run-and-tumble bacteria under chemotaxis, active swimmers, and animal movement
L000677	\cite{Saito2025, Karani2019, Codutti2019, Popescu2018, Buness2024, Sourjik2012, Mlynarczyk2019, Nieuwenhuizen2004, McKenzie2009, Boissard2013, Lauga2006, Kummel2013, Schneirla1944, Narazaki2021, Wang2013}. Finally, mapping the dynamics onto Eq.\,\ref{Langevin}

L000679	$\beta({\bf x})$ from experimentally observed trajectories.

L000681	In summary, we presented a novel theory for the MFPT of velocity jump processes
L000682	in higher dimensions, whose general form is
L000683	Eq.\,\ref{MFPT}.  For fixed speed and the angular distributions
L000684	listed in Table \ref{table1} for $d=2,3$, we show that the capture statistics in the small Knudsen number limit are governed by the bias terms $\alpha(\bx)$ and $\beta(\bx)$ via Eq.\,\ref{superfinal}, and
L000685	can differ quite significantly
L000686	from those observed under standard diffusion. Furthermore, the identification of a generator function
L000687	for the underlying stochastic process leads to the Langevin approximation in Eq.\,\ref{Langevin}
L000688	that efficiently describes the transport dynamics.
L000689	We fixed particle speed and let directional persistence arise from the sharpness of the angular distribution. If particle speeds followed heavy-tailed distributions, as in L\'evy processes, exceptionally large jumps could lead to rare boundary-reaching events. This scenario would require a different analysis than what presented here, invoking for example the “single big jump” principle \cite{Vezzani2019}. Solving the full problem in Eq.\,\ref{backward} requires tracking both particle position and velocity. Appropriate boundary conditions must be specified for $S({\bf x}, {\bf v}, t)$, carefully distinguishing between inward and outward directions on the boundary, as shown in the SM. A full treatment is left for future work.
